newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian officials call Kashmir polls a victory.
newsitem.headline: Indian officials call Kashmir polls a victory.

text.p: Indian authorities said on Saturday that troubled Kashmir's first local elections since the outbreak of a separatist rebellion represented a peaceful triumph of democracy over militancy.
But the first assembly polls in Jammu and Kashmir state since 1987 were marred by widespread reports that security officers forced some voters to cast ballots.
The elections were also disrupted by heavy cross-border firing across the ceasefire line between Indian and Pakistani-held Kashmir and the deaths of at least four people in scattered violence.
Indian rules two-thirds and Pakistan the remaining third of Kashmir, over which the two countries have fought two of their three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.
Officials said between 50 and 53 percent of eligible voters turned out in the local polls, slightly higher than the 49 percent who cast ballots in general elections in May.

"The process has been completed very satisfactorily," the state's chief secretary Ashok Kumar told reporters. "The people of the state have proved that they want their own representatives to form the government, they want a restoration of democracy."

At least four people, including three youths, died on the first of four days of polling spread over September. Twenty-six of 87 constituencies voted on Saturday, and polling in the others will take place on September 16, 21 and 30.

Indian and Pakistani troops exchanged fire in at least four places along their 830-km (520-mile) long Himalayan border, Indian defence officials said. Cross-border shooting is common but an Indian army spokesman said the firing was heavier than usual and in more places.

"We have concluded the day without any loss of life or injury to anybody from the polling machinery, from the political parties' candidates and from the mass of voters," chief electoral officer J.A. Khan said.
Khan said voters had defied threats from militant groups which had vowed to punish voters.

State police chief M.N. Saberwal said 29 separatists, including Shabir Shah, sometimes called "the Nelson Mandela of Kashmir", were detained or placed under house arrest to prevent them from deterring voters from going to the polls.

Most separatist groups had urged voters to boycott the polls, viewed as crucial to Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's efforts to restore democracy in the state, where more than 20,000 people have been killed since early 1990.

Voters in several localities said security personnel forced them to cast ballots. Witnesses said paramilitary troopers were seen knocking on voters' doors and police were seen escorting some people to polling stations in buses.

"Early in the morning the army came to our village and forced us to go two miles away from our village to cast our vote," said Mohammad Ashraf, who had come from Tangdi Bala village to Baramulla town, 50 km (30 miles) from Srinagar.
But authorities shrugged off allegations of coercion. "By and large, polling has been free from any of the malpractices generally related to the conduct of elections," Khan said.

In Pakistan-controlled Kashmir local leader Sultan Mahmood led hundreds of marchers to a U.N. military observers' office in Muzaffarabad to hand a memorandum protesting against the elections and calling for a U.N.-mandated plebiscite in Kashmir.
"Kashmiris have rejected these elections (in Indian Kashmir) and will continue their struggle until freedom," Mahmood said in a speech to Muzaffarabad protesters.
